title: Sarde a Beccafico
author: Marco Bellini
desc: Butterflied sardines rolled around a sweet, breadcrumb-and-pine-nut stuffing, baked until golden — named for their resemblance to the plump little songbird once considered a delicacy.
longDesc: This elaborate Sicilian preparation transforms humble sardines into an elegant dish, each fillet stuffed and rolled, arranged upright in a spiral in the baking dish so they resemble a nest — a presentation as deliberate as the sweet-savory filling itself.
ingredients: 16 fresh sardines, cleaned, butterflied, and boned
40 g (¼ cup) raisins, soaked in warm water
60 ml (¼ cup) extra virgin olive oil, plus more for drizzling
steps: Combine the toasted breadcrumbs, pine nuts, drained raisins, minced anchovy, parsley, garlic, and lemon zest with a drizzle of olive oil to bind into a coarse, moist filling.
Lay each butterflied sardine flat, skin-side down, and season lightly.
Place a spoonful of filling at one end of each sardine and roll up tightly from head to tail.
Arrange the rolled sardines upright, seam-side down, in a baking dish, packing them closely together in a spiral pattern.
Tuck a bay leaf between some of the rolls for aroma.
Drizzle generously with olive oil and scatter any remaining filling over the top.
Bake at 200°C (400°F) for 15–20 minutes until golden and cooked through.
Serve warm or at room temperature with lemon wedges.
chefTips: Ask your fishmonger to butterfly and bone the sardines if you're not confident doing this yourself, as it takes some practice.
Pack the rolled sardines tightly in the dish so they support each other and hold their shape while baking.
This dish is traditionally served just warm or at room temperature, not piping hot.
commonMistakes: Overfilling each sardine, making them difficult to roll neatly and causing the filling to spill out.
Overbaking, which dries out the delicate sardines.
Rushing the boning process, leaving bones that make the dish unpleasant to eat.
reheating: Best served at room temperature; if reheating, do so gently to avoid drying out the fish.
healthBenefits: Sardines are rich in omega-3 fatty acids, calcium, and vitamin D.
culturalNote: Sarde a beccafico takes its name from a small songbird once considered a delicacy in Sicily, the rolled sardines said to resemble the bird's plump shape.
